📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The first 11 games of the Serie A season have produced some rather intriguing trends regarding AC Milan’s attacking productivity.
  • MilanNews recall how – after the important win in Genoa before the break – Ruben Amorim emphasised how this Milan team are still far from the final product he envisioned in the summer, especially in the final third.
  • Sources indicate that the Rossoneri are improving in possession control and chance creation, but they often remain too far from the opponent’s penalty area for most of the game.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The first 11 games of the Serie A season have produced some rather intriguing trends regarding AC Milan’s attacking productivity.

MilanNews recall how – after the important win in Genoa before the break – Ruben Amorim emphasised how this Milan team are still far from the final product he envisioned in the summer, especially in the final third.

Sources indicate that the Rossoneri are improving in possession control and chance creation, but they often remain too far from the opponent’s penalty area for most of the game. This limitation has also affected Gonçalo Ramos, who has been forced to drop deeper, far away from the penalty box.

After 11 league games, Milan are only 17th in Serie A for shots on goal, averaging 11.5 per game. Yet, they lead Serie A in average xG per shot, at 0.145. In other words, the Rossoneri do not shoot much, but when they do it is very dangerous.

This is also confirmed by the remarkable individual numbers. Adrien Rabiot has scored five goals from 12 shots, with a conversion rate of 41.7%. Diego Moreira is at 40%, Alphadjo Cisse at 38.5%, and Christian Pulisic at 36.4%.

Recent findings suggest that the notable absentee from this ranking is the player expected to score the most: Gonçalo Ramos. The Portuguese has scored just three goals with 33 total shots and 5.35 xG, meaning a conversion rate of 9.1%. These numbers are far from those of his team-mates.

Recent findings suggest that amorim continues to defend him, emphasising that the problem lies primarily with the team being too deep. Milan must therefore start to generate more territorial dominance, to allow Ramos to operate closer to goal and for him to be on the end of what is clearly quality service being provided.

Welcome to another Arsecast Extra, the Arsenal podcast, with myself and James from @gunnerblog.

In a recent development, in this episode we look back at the 1-0 win over Hull on Saturday. There were some first half moments, but the two big incidents involved Kai Havertz – and we discuss his big chance and the penalty he should have been awarded. There’s also praise for Noni Madueke who kept trying to make things happen and whose shot led to the only goal of the game from Martin Odegaard, before he fluffed his own lines in front of goal when he should have scored. In part two we have listener questions about Mikel Arteta’s obvious frustration with Eberechi Eze, whether it’s sustainable to keep winning by single goal margins, Christos Tzolis and what he’s brought to the team so far, our attacking play, recognising our quality and lots more.

Interlull musings and shiny distractions

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1038 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that we’re two days into the final Interlull of the year and, as you might expect, there’s not a huge amount going on.
  • This time around, 20 of our 25 first-team players have been selected, which is a pretty remarkable tally.
  • According to recent reports, any concerns about the Frenchman’s absence against Hull, having travelled to Prague in midweek, were eased the following morning when he lined up for the under-21s against Aston Villa in Premier League 2.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we’re two days into the final Interlull of the year and, as you might expect, there’s not a huge amount going on. The senior fixtures don’t start until Thursday, so we haven’t even got a fresh batch of international press conference quotes to sink our teeth into. Slim pickings.

This time around, 20 of our 25 first-team players have been selected, which is a pretty remarkable tally. All the more so when you consider Noni Madueke can count himself unlucky to have missed out for England, while Bukayo Saka and William Saliba would ordinarily be shoo-ins.

According to recent reports, any concerns about the Frenchman’s absence against Hull, having travelled to Prague in midweek, were eased the following morning when he lined up for the under-21s against Aston Villa in Premier League 2. More minutes in his legs, rather than another injury to worry about.

According to recent reports, bolstered by Saliba and Max Dowman, whose domestic suspension kept him out of Saturday’s game, the youngsters ran out 5-2 winners. Given they’re presently 21st out of 31 teams in their Swiss-style league table, perhaps this is the way forward. Send the major guns down a level and start battering our way towards more club silverware. Relentless madman Arteta, finding newly introduced frontiers for his evil genius. He doesn’t just leave his technical area. He thinks outside it.

If you missed it, Max has been promoted to England’s under-21s for this window. He’ll join Arsenal loanees Tommy Setford and Ethan Nwaneri, as well as former Hale Enders Brooke Norton-Cuffy, who came off the bench for Hull on Saturday, and Amario Cozier-Duberry, who seems to be doing well at Middlesbrough on loan from Brighton.

Sources indicate that given Max has been in and around Mikel Arteta’s first team for a couple of seasons now, it’s easy to take milestones like this for granted. But playing under-21 international football at 16 is another significant step, even for someone whose talent has made rapid progress seem almost routine.

Back in September, Lee Carsley described his eventual promotion as inevitable, while stressing that the timing had to be right. The point was to bring him into a squad where he could play and compete, rather than move him up simply because everyone expected it.

Carsley referenced Nwaneri when discussing the temptation to push exceptional youngsters through the age groups. His point was that the aim is a long senior career, not winning a race to the first cap. That seems sensible enough. Max doesn’t need every appearance to become an audition for the next level.

According to recent reports, A couple of games against Portugal and France should be a useful challenge in their own right. Carsley and Arteta also know each other from their Everton days, which ought to help when discussing what he needs.

According to recent reports, with England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland hosting Euro 2028, you can imagine that tournament already features somewhere in Max’s ambitions. There’s plenty of football between now and then, though. For the moment, let’s see how he gets on with this next step.

Elsewhere, most of our European internationals will be occupied with the Nations League, while the South American trio rack up the air miles again. Piero Hincapie heads home to Ecuador for friendlies against Costa Rica and Bolivia, while Gabriel and Bruno Guimaraes face Japan and Singapore, both in Singapore.

It has been revealed that I appreciate Brazil’s options are more limited when European teams are tied up with UEFA fixtures, but their friendly schedule does sometimes feel like somebody has thrown a dart at a map. No doubt the commercial logic is compelling, but that doesn’t make you any less worried about tired hamstrings.

Anyway, fingers crossed they all come back with their limbs intact.

In other news, Italian publication Tuttosport has named Andrea Berta the winner of its Best Executive Award at this year’s Golden Boy Awards. The Arsenal sporting director collects the gong three transfer windows into his tenure, the latest of which ended with some fans calling for his head after the failed pursuits of Vinicius Junior and Julian Alvarez.

Industry observers note that either the bar is pretty low, he’s basking in the reflected glory of the team’s success, or it’s one of those shindigs where buying an inordinately expensive table guarantees you something shiny to take home. The cynic in me wasn’t exactly silenced by the news that Joan Laporta won Best President and Jorge Mendes Best Agent. In fact, I snorted when I read that. And lest we forget, Edu picked up a similar award from the same organisers in 2023….

In a recent development, myles Lewis-Skelly was in contention for the actual Golden Boy award, which went to Barcelona defender Pau Cubarsi. Hard to argue too much with that, given the 19-year-old was at the heart of Spain’s World Cup win.

According to recent reports, cubarsi also made the FIFPRO World 11. More pertinently for us, so did David Raya. Having finished second to compatriot Unai Simon in the Ballon d’Or’s Best Goalkeeper category, I imagine there’s some satisfaction in getting the nod from the people who actually play the game. More than 26,000 professionals from 75 countries cast their votes, which is a fairly substantial dressing room to win over.

Alessia Russo, who is in fine form even if Arsenal Women are not, also earned her third selection for the Women’s World 11.

As you’ll have gathered from the snippiness above, I find it easy to be cynical about these things. There are so many awards now that you half expect to get one for finding your seat at the ceremony. Still, sometimes it’s nice to give people a pat on the back and recognise a job well done.

On an entirely unrelated note, have you voted for us to win Best Fan Media at the upcoming FSA Awards? You’ve only got a week left. A prestigious honour, that one. 😉.

Right, I think that’s as much toothpaste as I can squeeze out of a slow news day. If anything else happens, we’ll have it covered on Arseblog News. Catch you next time.

Liverpool vs. Man Utd trophies: Who has won more honours?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1249 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Barney Corkhill | 20 Nov 2026 23:32.
  • According to recent reports, liverpool have won more major trophies than Manchester United, leading the Liverpool vs.
  • With a margin that small, the answer depends on what you count, because leaving out the one-off 1986 Football League Super Cup puts the clubs level, while leaving out the Community Shield gives the Reds a clear lead.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Barney Corkhill | 20 Nov 2026 23:32.

According to recent reports, liverpool have won more major trophies than Manchester United, leading the Liverpool vs. Man Utd trophies count 69-68 on every senior competitive honour as of November 20, 2026.

With a margin that small, the answer depends on what you count, because leaving out the one-off 1986 Football League Super Cup puts the clubs level, while leaving out the Community Shield gives the Reds a clear lead.

Neither club has lifted a trophy since Liverpool's 2024-25 Premier League title, which nudged the Anfield outfit back ahead of their eternal rivals.

Liverpool and Manchester United share the record for English league titles with 20 each, after the Merseysiders' 2024-25 Premier League win matched the total the Red Devils reached in 2012-13.

United are stronger in the FA Cup, with 13 wins to Liverpool's eight, and in the Community Shield, which they have won or shared 21 times against 16 for the Anfield club.

Liverpool hold the record of 10 League Cups, four more than their rivals, and they are the only one of the pair to have won the Football League Super Cup, which was played only once.

The gap opens up in Europe, where six European Cups, three UEFA Cups and four UEFA Super Cups give the Reds 13 continental trophies to United's six.

Liverpool have more trophies than Manchester United on the fullest count, one ahead, and they also lead when Community Shields are left out.

United only draw level if the 1986 Football League Super Cup is removed or shared Community Shields are discounted, and they only go ahead on a count limited to the league, FA Cup and League Cup, which they lead 39-38.

That makes the Reds the more decorated club, since they lead or are level on every method that includes European competition, and the only count that favours the Old Trafford side ignores continental silverware altogether.

United's honours board leaves out the Super Cup and so indicates the rivals level, which is a fair reading, but even on that basis the Red Devils still need one more trophy to go ahead.

Opinion is split on whether the Community Shield should count as a genuine trophy, and the FA itself treats it as a friendly for disciplinary purposes, so bookings in it do not carry over into other domestic games.

The fixture has only been contested between the league champions and the FA Cup winners since 1974, and before that it was an invitational match.

Seven of United's Community Shields and three of Liverpool's came before that change, which strengthens the case for leaving the trophy out.

The Anfield club's own honours page lists 52 major men's honours, a figure that excludes both the Community Shield and the Football League Super Cup, and the Community Shield never appeared on the honours board at their old Melwood training ground either.

Counting the Football League Super Cup but not the Community Shield gives the Reds a 53-47 lead, a six-trophy cushion over the Red Devils.

The Football League Super Cup was set up after the Heysel Stadium disaster in May 1985 and the European ban on English clubs that followed, as a replacement competition for the six sides who would have played on the continent in 1985-86.

Liverpool beat Everton in a two-legged final held back until September 1986, winning 3-1 at Anfield and 4-1 at Goodison Park for a 7-2 aggregate victory.

The tournament was never played again, which is why some honours boards ignore it, and counting it or not decides whether the Merseysiders lead or the clubs are level.

A drawn Community Shield used to be shared, and Liverpool's list includes five shared editions (1964, 1965, 1977, 1986 and 1990), while United shared four (1965, 1967, 1977 and 1990).

The years 1965, 1977 and 1990 appear on both lists, and removing every shared Community Shield leaves both clubs on 64, another count where Man United can claim a tie but not a lead.

Manchester United have their strongest case at home, with 60 domestic honours to Liverpool's 55 when Community Shields and the Football League Super Cup are counted.

In the three main domestic competitions, the league, FA Cup and League Cup, the Red Devils lead 39-38 thanks to five more FA Cup wins.

Cup finals between the pair have been split evenly, as United won the 1977 FA Cup final 2-1 and the 1996 final 1-0, while the Reds won the League Cup finals of 1983 and 2003.

The 1983 final went to extra time, with Alan Kennedy and Ronnie Whelan cancelling out Norman Whiteside's opener for a 2-1 win, and Steven Gerrard and Michael Owen scored in the 2-0 win in Cardiff 20 years later.

Sources indicate that for every result between the two clubs rather than just the silverware, our Man Utd vs. Liverpool head-to-head record covers each meeting.

Liverpool's six European Cups are more than any other British team has won and double United's three, and that record is what separates the clubs.

The Reds add three UEFA Cups and four UEFA Super Cups, while United's six European trophies are completed by a Europa League, a Cup Winners' Cup and one UEFA Super Cup.

United edge the world honours 2-1, having won the 1999 Intercontinental Cup and the 2008 Club World Cup, while the Merseysiders won the Club World Cup in 2019.

For the stories behind several of those European nights, including the 2005 final in Istanbul, our rundown of Liverpool's 10 greatest comebacks goes back through the club's most dramatic recoveries.

Manchester United's modern haul was built under Sir Alex Ferguson, who won 38 trophies in 26 years in charge between 1986 and 2013, including 13 league titles, five FA Cups and two Champions League titles.

The teams behind that run feature heavily in our ranking of Manchester United's 10 greatest ever teams, which sets the Ferguson sides against the club's earlier eras.

The latest swings came in 2023-24, when Liverpool's League Cup win put them one ahead on the full count before the Red Devils beat Manchester City in the FA Cup final to draw level again.

The Reds' 2024-25 Premier League title then put them one clear, while on the count that ignores the Super Cup the same sequence went from a tie to a United lead and back to the current tie.

Liverpool and Manchester United are both in the 2026-27 Champions League league phase, so Europe offers the biggest single swing, alongside the FA Cup, the League Cup and the next Community Shield.

One trophy for United without a reply from Anfield would level the full count, while any Liverpool success would stretch the gap to two.

Liverpool appear to have a better chance of adding to their haul in the 2026-27 campaign, with Man United out of the League Cup and having seen any faint hopes of a title challenge evaporate amidst their worst-ever start to a Premier League season.

The Old Trafford side are now led by Mauricio Pochettino, who became head coach in November 2026 after Michael Carrick was sacked.

To see what the newly introduced head coach brings, our breakdown of Pochettino's record against every Premier League club demonstrates how his past teams have fared against each top-flight side.

For a view of current strength rather than history, our ranking of the best football teams in the world shows where Liverpool sit among Europe's elite.

Liverpool are at the centre of an exciting move, and it could be for a bargain.

If there is one thing Andoni Iraola will be disappointed by during his start to life at Anfield it's the lack of creativity in his attack.

Industry observers note that the club's recruitment team has assembled an exciting cohort of attackers. Yet aside from Alexander Isak, none of them appear to be thriving too much in front of goal.

In fact, Liverpool could be a lot worse off if it was not for Isak's efficiency who is very much putting away most of his chances at the moment.

But statistically, Liverpool are struggling to create chances, and this is due to the accumulation of various factors.

It's something that has to be addressed in the market, but there could be internal solutions as well.

Recent findings suggest that why are Liverpool struggling to create chances?A lot of people have pinned the blame on Florian Wirtz. He is after all the chief architect at the club. But Liverpool's problems are not simply down to Wirtz not pulling his weight. If you're looking at Liverpool's attackers with the exception of Bradley Barcola, most of them are attackers who want to cut into the middle. And then behind them there is not enough offensive output from the full-backs on the wings. Milos Kerkez is not a super creative player neither is Ronald Araujo. Both have their uses for various other reasons. However, ultimately, Liverpool could be better off recruiting more technical full-backs who are capable of producing chances and playing passes promptly into their teammates. The same can be said for the midfield, where Liverpool are missing a more creative force.

#72042. Zubimendi addresses tiredness and transfer talk

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1286 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arseblog ↗ Open Full Page

Zubimendi addresses tiredness and transfer talk

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1286 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Martin’s Day in Germany, a day I’d never heard of until I had a child over here.
  • Martin was, as the story goes, a 4th-Century Roman soldier and is best known for sharing his cloak with a freezing beggar.
  • Fitting, then, that Martin Zubimendi should be linked with a move to Chelsea (and others).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Good morning all, hope you’re well! It’s St. Martin’s Day in Germany, a day I’d never heard of until I had a child over here. Kids will leave Kindergarten and chant as they walk through their neighbourhoods with lanterns this evening, as is tradition. Doesn’t sound creepy at all, does it?

Sources indicate that st. Martin was, as the story goes, a 4th-Century Roman soldier and is best known for sharing his cloak with a freezing beggar.

Fitting, then, that Martin Zubimendi should be linked with a move to Chelsea (and others). It would be the saintly thing to do to share some of our midfield spoils with the desperate, downtrodden, shivering squad that Xabi Alonso has at his disposal. I hope we let them get absolutely glacial – Siberian, even, given their history – and keep our glorious cloak of midfielders all to ourselves.

Recent findings suggest that the first rule of the international break is, of course, to ignore all transfer rumours. Club football goes away but there are still pages to fill, newspapers to sell, online traffic to amass, and something has to fill the void.

And, speaking to Marca, the midfielder has denied that he’s unhappy:.

I’m calm and happy with how I’m handling this situation. (Not playing) is something I’ve never experienced before, and I think you learn from these situations too.

Industry observers note that I’m patient. When you’ve been playing a lot of minutes and your role changes to not playing as much, I’m able to see the positive side. I think everything passes, that just like last year the opposite happened to me and I played practically everything, this can change very quickly.

Asked about the toll that playing so much took on him last season – Zubimendi was the only Arsenal player to play in all 38 Premier League games, he started 34 of those and had the third most minutes in the squad, behind David Raya and Declan Rice, across all competitions – he admitted that that was a factor:.

I don’t like to blame everything on my physical condition, but I definitely noticed it that year. It was a upcoming year for me, with a lot of new stimuli. I played a huge number of minutes and, to be honest, I was tired. Then there were other things too, but one of them could very well have been my physical condition.

Sources indicate that I spoke with Mikel at the beginning of the season. As he does with all the players, he explained the blueprint to me. He warned me that there were new signings and that there would be playing time for everyone. And here we are, fighting for it.

And he completely dismissed any suggestion that he is talking to other clubs, given those links to the Madrid sides and Chelsea:.

I haven’t wasted any energy on outside things. I’m busy enough trying to earn a place, get playing time, and fight to win this Premier League, which is looking so promising. I haven’t spent any energy on it, nor have I contacted anyone.

To be honest, I’m sometimes surprised by the press too. I understand that the winter transfer window is approaching and rumours can surface, but I think we need to be a bit more careful with what we publish. Ultimately, everyone has a team they play for, and we need to respect that. I’ve also read that I might be close (to a transfer), but not at all.

Still, I do think the case of Zubimendi is an interesting one. Having lost his place late last season, he returned late in the summer, and is yet to start a Premier League game in 2026-27 following the emergence of Myles Lewis-Skelly and the arrival of Bruno Guimaraes.

In a recent development, here we have a player Arsenal desperately wanted and agreed a deal for a year ahead of signing him, would they really be looking to move him on again now that he’s spent what is essentially just a quarter of a season not as first choice? So much focus has been placed on building a squad that can sustain injuries or absences, and then we’d leave ourselves light again?

Maybe? You never can know how transfers pan out ahead of time, and things can change rapidly in football but, as Zubimendi suggests, they can change quickly in the other direction again too. Did anyone, for instance, envisage Lewis-Skelly starting against Atletico Madrid just a week before it actually happened?

Industry observers note that I do think his particular rise, and a stressful second half of the season, has clouded what we all thought of Zubimendi’s first half-season at Arsenal, and how much he contributed across the entire campaign. At this stage a year ago, we were two points worse off than we are now but still top of the league by six points, with more goals scored and fewer goals conceded than we are 10 games in this time around. He was a massive part of that.

Recent findings suggest that he was a huge part of winning the title and reaching the Champions League final – he started 43 of our 53 games across those two competitions. He started every Champions League knockout game up until the semi-final second leg and played all of extra-time in the final.

And if he was suffering physically, there was no break in the summer, as he went off to the World Cup, Spain went all the way, and he was back on the pitch for Arsenal (having had no pre-season) in Cardiff as we won the Community Shield, less than a month on from the World Cup final.

For all that, I can also see why someone would possibly want to make the case for moving on. Seeing a player not be used (Zubimendi has played in seven of our league games so far this season, by the way!) feels like an obvious place to upgrade, and we’ve been scarred before by letting players sit on the bench before then struggling to move them on for a fair fee.

We’re also going to need to refresh the age of the team and especially the midfield before long. When you don’t just look at the players themselves but actually account for who is playing the minutes, we have the third-oldest squad in the league this season. The frontline will need new faces soon – that’s not news to anyone – in terms of age as well as quality, but the midfield will need it on the age front as well.

We’ve also given the fewest minutes in the league to players under the age of 23 (around 6%) by some distance. If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it, but if you don’t get the balance right it will break in time.

In a recent development, right now, though, this season, we’re likely to need our whole squad. We can’t be making it weaker. If one of Declan Rice – God forbid – or Bruno Guimaraes were to pick up a knock and miss a month, Zubimendi would suddenly be in line for a lot of football. Zubimendi who, again, was central to us winning the league last season.

It’s far too soon into the season to write his campaign off, especially when we saw how things changed so suddenly in that exact position back in May. Let’s see how things look when the summer rolls around, but there’s no need to rush into a decision.

Right then, have a great day all – and I’ll leave you with the gorgeous generosity of another St. Martin close to our hearts.

#72039. The virtues of patience

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1349 w)
📖 Baca

The virtues of patience

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1349 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it’s 13 December 2020.
  • In a recent development, it was freezing and wet at the Emirates.
  • It has been revealed that this was supposed to be fun.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Let’s take a journey back in time.

According to recent reports, it’s 13 December 2020. Arsenal versus Burnley.

In a recent development, it was freezing and wet at the Emirates. Only 2,000 fans had been allowed in because of Covid, and my mum, my dad, my mate Ben and I made up four of them. We were socially distanced and wearing masks. My glasses kept steaming up.

It has been revealed that this was supposed to be fun. Watching my team.

Willian was grotesquely slow. Alex Lacazette was profligate. Rob Holding was bald. Very bald. And Granit Xhaka was angry. So angry, in fact, that in the second half he put his hands around the throat of some opposition goon and, after a VAR review, got himself sent off. There were boos. As many as 2,000 people could muster, anyway.

Then our captain, Pierre Emerick-Aubameyang, headed a corner into his own net. You couldn’t make it up. Except you could. It was the only goal of the game.

By then the steam fogging up my specs might as well have been coming out of my ears. In his player ratings, Andrew M called Xhaka the ‘King of the Idiots’ and described the match and the result as ‘utterly shit’. Which was fair.

It has been revealed that it was our seventh defeat in 10 league games and our fourth in a row at home, something that hadn’t happened since 1953. We were 15th, five points above the relegation zone.

It has been revealed that and who was top? Sp*rs. Managed by everyone’s favourite sociopath, Jose Mourinho. Having beaten us in the North London derby the week before, they couldn’t stop gloating.

Sources indicate that I’d bought into the Arteta project hook, line and sinker. I still wanted him to be the right man for the job. I was just finding it harder to explain why I thought he was. The FA Cup win had been four months earlier. It felt like years.

The tree, to paraphrase our manager, was shaking.

It had been shaking for a good two and a half years by then. The soggy bottom of the Arsene Wenger era had left its scars. Those two 3-0 defeats to City in the space of a week still make me wince. Then came the hope that Unai Emery might get us back on track. By the time we’d seen how that played out, I’d got into the habit of talking myself down whenever things looked up. Maybe we’ll get better. Give it time.

Industry observers note that the trouble with rock bottom is you never know if there’s another floor below it. Was Burnley ours? I’m still writing about it six years later, so it was probably mine. There were games against Southampton and Everton before Christmas, and I can barely remember either of them.

Sources indicate that then came Boxing Day and a visit from Frank Lampard’s Chelsea. Is it reductive to say that was the day everything changed for Mikel Arteta’s Arsenal? Probably. But my word, watching Bukayo Saka, Emile Smith Rowe and Gabriel Martinelli tear about the place was the fix this addict needed. We went on an unbeaten run after that. Seven whole games! And for the first time in weeks, I was looking forward to what came next.

According to recent reports, and here we are in November 2026. Reigning champions of England. Top of the league again. Five points clear. Odds-on favourites to retain the title after 10 games. Sure, throwing hundreds of millions of American dollars at the problem helped. But if there’s a lesson in all this, it’s that hard work and patience pay off.

Which is why I’m using today’s blog to appeal directly to Sir Jim Ratcliffe to give Michael Carrick a stay of execution.

Come on, man, you’re probably still paying off Erik ten Hag and Ruben Amorim, maybe even Ralf Rangnick. Do you really want to go back to the drawing board all over again? Carrick is the man for the Manchester United hot seat. Just look at the way he wore a poppy-embroidered armband as well as a poppy badge at the weekend. The man doesn’t do half measures. He’s a two-scoops guy. Surely that’s something you, a multibillionaire British-born petrochemicals tycoon who lives in Monaco, can get on board with?

Sources indicate that I know Mauricio Pochettino might be tempting. He’s got floppy hair, a tan and, despite the Sp*rsy stench, has come to resemble a rather huggable teddy bear. But think it through, Jim. What if he comes in and everybody perks up? It’s much harder to make job cuts and to force out season ticket holders when people are enjoying themselves. Best get through that process first while Michael turns the oil tanker round. It’s not far off, promise, you’re on a two-game unbeaten streak!

Anyway, what would sacking Carrick say about patience? Look at Arteta. There were people who wanted him gone after Burnley and, as you’ve just read, I was close to joining them. Imagine if the club had listened to me. All those years of work, all that progress, all the joy I’ve had watching Arsenal lately. We could have thrown it all away because a man in a damp mask couldn’t see out of his glasses.

It has been revealed that so give Carrick time. Give him January. Give him a full pre-season. And if things still haven’t picked up by this time next year, ask yourself whether one full pre-season, and £100 million on Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos, was ever really enough.

I can only speak for myself, Jim, but I haven’t looked forward to watching Manchester United this much in years.

Right, let’s see if that works….

According to recent reports, the Interlull kicks into gear tonight. David Raya, Mikel Merino and Martin Zubimendi are in action for Spain against Czechia, Riccardo Calafiori’s Italy take on France, and England face Croatia at Wembley.

According to recent reports, ezri Konsa and Myles Lewis-Skelly will both miss out at Wembley. Konsa is working on his fitness but will be available to face Spain on Sunday, while our Hale Ender is suspended after picking up two bookings in the Nations League.

Industry observers note that elsewhere, ahead of Sweden’s game against Bosnia and Herzegovina, Viktor Gyokeres has been speaking to the press. Like Martin Zubimendi, he notes he’s happy at Arsenal.

“I want to,” he stated, when asked if he’s keen to stay at the Emirates.

Sources indicate that “It feels good when I’ve played. We’ve won most of the games. It was a tough loss in the cup (against Fleetwood). Otherwise it’s felt good for myself and the team, says the forward. I’ve been doing well lately when I’ve been playing. Right now it feels good.

“The communication with (Mikel) Arteta is good. We talk about football and how we should play. Before a match, if I’m going to start, we talk about the opponents and what I should think about.”.

He was also asked whether the criticism he gets bothers him.

It has been revealed that “Sometimes it might get to me, but overall not so much. If I score goals and assists in the Champions League, I couldn’t care less what they say. It’s nice to do those kinds of performances. To deliver for myself and for the team. That’s where the focus lies.”.

Recent findings suggest that to be fair, I’ve not seen any serious chatter about selling Viktor in January. Whatever you think of him as a player, it would be a strange move unless we’re planning to spend serious money on the attack. And even then it would feel like an unnecessary risk given Kai isn’t exactly pulling up trees and new faces will need an adaptation period.

If he’s happy keeping his head down and doing his bit for the team, I’d keep him around until the summer and reassess then.

Ok. I’m going to leave it there for today. All eyes on Old Trafford, I guess.

Liverpool believe a 6ft5 star might actually grow even further. He's going to be a monster.

Liverpool have spent the last few years amassing as much elite talent as possible. That's mainly seen in the substantial-money signings like Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola.

According to recent reports, those three are all nine-figure signings and among the most expensive players in history. But it's not the only way Liverpool have gone about their plan.

They've also moved for young players. Those with elite-level talent and who require a push in the right direction to place them among the best in the world. Jeremy Jacquet might be the most obvious example in Liverpool's first-team right now.

According to recent reports, but there is another who we've been waiting to see. And Liverpool feel he hasn't even finished developing physically.

In a recent development, jacquet might be the star centre-back of the future right now but he wasn't a little over a year ago. Back then it was Giovanni Leoni, who arrived from Parma with incredible hype.

Sources indicate that however, Leoni would suffer a terrible knee injury on his debut, meaning he still hasn't actually completed 90 minutes for Liverpool. He hasn't played since, either, and only got back to training with teammates this week.

Recent findings suggest that liverpool are managing Leoni's comeback very, very carefully. That would be the case anyway, of course, but there's an extra reason to do so here as The Times reports that the club feel he might still be growing.

Recent findings suggest that that complicates his recovery process but it also slightly surreal to hear as Leoni is already 6ft5. He's a massive defender as it is but it appears the 19-year-old may get even more massive.

Sources indicate that growth like that can have negative effects. It generates extra pressure on joints, means players carry weight differently, and can lead to complications. Of course, it can also have positive effects like a player who towers over forwards and doesn't even need to jump particularly high to win headers.

We'll see how things land with that one.

By Ben Sully | 20 Nov 2026 23:38, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 02:10.

Liverpool captain Virgil van Dijk has admitted he has "no idea" about whether he will be at Anfield beyond the end of the season.

Van Dijk has established himself as a Liverpool icon in his 389 appearances since joining the club from Southampton in 2018.

The Dutchman has helped the Merseyside club win numerous pieces of silverware, including two Premier League titles and the 2018-19 Champions League.

However, it is unclear how much longer he will play a part in Liverpool's quest for trophies, with his current contract set to expire at the end of the campaign.

Van Dijk recently commented on his situation while on international duty, insisting that he is "not in any panic" over his Anfield future.

The centre-back has reiterated his relaxed outlook in an interview with Sky Sports, in which he conceded he has "no idea" whether he will sign a latest Liverpool deal.

"The main thing for me is that I feel good and I'm looking after myself and I still have many more years in my opinion," Van Dijk mentioned.

"Whatever's going to happen after this season, we'll see.

"At this moment of time, if anyone says that or put out that they know what I'm going to do next season, it's untrue because at this moment of time, speaking to you, I've got no idea either.

"But I'm relaxed with it because if you know me, I only focus on what I can control and that's at the moment the Manchester United game.

"Then we'll focus to the Champions League and whatever happens in the newly introduced year coming, we'll see then.

"But it's been an incredible journey, almost 10 years this summer and it's been a big part of my life and I'll forever be grateful for anything that happened over those years.

Recent findings suggest that "If it's getting extended, we'll see then. If not, then I'm going to say goodbyes in the summer.".

At the age of 35, Van Dijk remains an integral part of the Liverpool squad, demonstrated by the fact he has played every minute of the club's 10 Premier League matches this term.

Van Dijk is now preparing to make his 350th Premier League appearance in Sunday's highly anticipated clash against rivals Manchester United.

The Netherlands international has made 282 of his 349 top-flight appearances in a Liverpool shirt after featuring in 67 Premier League matches for Southampton.

Van Dijk will hope to mark his milestone outing with a victory, although he has had to settle for seven wins in his previous 18 Premier League matches against Man United (D5, L6).

#72035. How Arsenal have evolved in 2026-27

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1315 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arseblog ↗ Open Full Page

How Arsenal have evolved in 2026-27

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1315 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There was a lot of speculation as to how Arsenal might change this season having flung a 22-year-old monkey (how long do monkeys live for?!) from their back in May by finally winning a league title.
  • I always had my doubts, not least because your style of play is always defined by your talent.
  • In attacking areas, he had talent, even if it wasn’t balanced.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There was a lot of speculation as to how Arsenal might change this season having flung a 22-year-old monkey (how long do monkeys live for?!) from their back in May by finally winning a league title. Would lifting the Premier League trophy lead to a new era of more expressive, urbane football?

I always had my doubts, not least because your style of play is always defined by your talent. Most of Arsenal’s elite talent is behind the ball. Arteta didn’t build Arsenal from the defence first, in my view, because he felt specifically that was the best way. It was just the area of the team that required the most attention when he was appointed.

In attacking areas, he had talent, even if it wasn’t balanced. Aubameyang, Lacazette and Pepe with Saka and Martinelli coming to the boil was a good collection of talent, even if the pieces didn’t always fit neatly together. The list of defenders he inherited included Mustafi, Sokratis, Holding, Chambers, Kolasinac and Mari. That’s why he went defence first, broadly speaking.

In a recent development, the moves the club have tried to make in recent seasons, especially this summer, shows you that Arteta wants his attack to be sharper than it is. For reasons I won’t relitigate here, the club were not able to add a number of high end attacking targets. Which means once again, Arsenal are reliant on Arteta’s coaching talents to squeeze more juice from the orange. Here are three things that have jumped out at me this season.

Arsenal spent a lot of money on Bruno Guimaraes this season and I will come onto some of the reasons why in the next section. But that signing has given Arteta a deep well of central options, with Rice, Bruno, Lewis Skelly, Odegaard, Merino and Zubimendi part of this midfield menagerie.

Arsenal use these options interchangeably and often according to game state. Art de Roche of the Athletic went into how Arteta has used the divergent profiles of Myles Lewis Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes so far in this campaign. In home games against Leeds and Everton, Lewis Skelly got the nod from the start.

According to recent reports, in away games at Nottingham Forest and Liverpool, Bruno’s more robust approach was favoured. The pair have made significant impacts from the bench too. When the 1-0 victory at Anfield had become a little too ‘basketball’, Lewis Skelly came on and provided calm assurance in possession.

In a recent development, when the Gunners needed a little more belligerence away at Sunderland, Bruno came on and larruped the ball into the top corner from 25 yards. However, Arteta didn’t part with a significant part of his summer budget for a 28-year-old (he turns 29 next week but, for now, he remains 28 because that’s how it works) to be a high level rotation option.

Recent findings suggest that against Hull City last weekend, Bruno was selected and he played deeper than Declan Rice and Martin Odegaard. As Adrian Clarke pointed out in his match analysis piece, Bruno passed the ball to Odegaard 25 times in that match and the pair exchanged 35 passes in total. The idea was clear, to use Bruno’s punchiness in possession a little lower to feed Odegaard.

In a recent development, against Everton, Mikel Merino was selected in midfield and Lewis Skelly started at left-back. I think this was about more than mere rotation. Arteta always highly respects the aerial capabilities of David Moyes’ Everton team, which makes sense since he played in a David Moyes Everton team for such a long time.

In 2023-24, Arteta selected Fabio Vieira ahead of Kai Havertz in midfield at Goodison Park because he wanted to keep the ball on the floor (Arsenal won that game 1-0 via a short corner routine because they did not see the logic of aerial corners against a team like Everton).

Sources indicate that last season at the Hill Dickinson Arsenal enjoyed a season high for passes attempted and completed because they wanted to keep the ball on the floor and avoid transitions. Arteta has a carousel available to him in midfield and a different club in the bag depending on what is called for on the day.

Per Opta, Arsenal have been caught offside 35 times so far this season, at least 11 more times than any other team. That rate of 3.5 offsides per game is the highest of any Premier League team since 2009. Kai Havertz has been flagged 15 times now, the next highest offender in the league is Dominic Calvert-Lewin with eight. Opta provide a deeper dive on those numbers here.

In a recent development, so what does this tell us, aside from the fact that Havertz needs to work on his timing? It means that Arsenal are far more willing to go in behind and they are willing to test the opposition backline earlier in moves. This was a substantial part of the reason they signed Bruno in the first place, Arteta wants to play with the risk reward dial with the ball.

Recent findings suggest that havertz also hasn’t been quite good enough to finish some of those one v one situations when he has got in behind the opponent’s back line. He fluffed his lines against Hull last weekend and in the 3-0 defeat at Brighton, he blasted his effort straight at the Brighton keeper when put through one v one.

In a recent development, but here, I will express my usual caveat, we need to normalise strikers missing chances and focus more on process than outcome. Most chances are missed, you want to worry when your striker is getting few shots. There have also been nascent signs that Arsenal have been using Gyokeres well in some of these situations.

It has been revealed that that Havertz chance at the Amex was created by Gyokeres taking one touch with his back to goal and hooking the ball past the committed defensive line. Gyokeres did much the same for Madueke in Prague. It seems like Arsenal have worked on getting Gyokeres to use his physicality to initially retain the ball- something he badly struggled with last season- but creating situations where he can release it promptly.

Sources indicate that arsenal’s out of possession prowess is one thing that has been a constant from last season. It is Arsenal’s superpower, so even when they can only manage one goal, it is usually enough to take maximum points. To retain their superpower, Arsenal changed to stay the same, if that makes sense.

According to recent reports, the signing of Ezri Konsa from Aston Villa was questioned by many but his presence has made the absence of a world class centre-back like William Saliba a sidebar, which is quite a feat. Arsenal ostensibly took William Saliba’s pizza chart and looked for the most Saliba like defender they could find and bought Konsa.

The loss of Saliba ought to have offered an enormous threat to Arsenal’s defensive stability. Arsenal’s tactical organisation out of possession is elite but so too are the individuals that helm it. Raya, Saliba, Gabriel and Rice are among the best players in the world in their respective positions.

It has been revealed that taking out one of those pillars ought to have derailed Arsenal’s defensive stability and it hasn’t because Konsa has the quality and poise to retain the team’s biggest strength. His pass completion stats are Saliba-esque and the quality of not giving the ball away needlessly is a significant part of the Gunners’ meanness.

Sources indicate that how much Arsenal could improve in attack without significant additions was an unknown so Arteta could not afford to sacrifice the team’s defensive ceiling while he plays with those levers. The addition of Konsa was a personnel change that allowed Arsenal to remain the same.

Sources indicate that greetings, Tim here on blog duty today and I am going right back to Arseblog’s roots by writing from Barcelona. I am here of course because Arsenal Women earned a very creditable (and slightly unexpected given how this season has gone for them) draw against the current Champions League holders Barcelona.

Of course, Renee Slegers’ side did beat Barca the last time the teams met in the 2025 Final and that was only slightly less of an upset than this result. As expected, Arsenal rose their luck a little with Barca putting up 24 shots and 2.4XG. But Arsenal have put up similar numbers in games this season roughly 176 times and not won so I am happy to be on the receiving end of a little serendipity.

Frida Maanum gave Arsenal a first half lead before her compatriot Caroline Graham Hansen equalised in the second half. You can read Renee Slegers’ post-match press conference here and my take on the match here if you are so inclined. Up next is a six pointer for Champions League qualification at home to London City Lionesses on Sunday which Arsenal just have to win. Obviously we will have all the usual coverage of that game for you.

I also had the pleasure of meeting fellow Arseblog / Arsenal Vision colleague Phil Costa for lunch and in Barcelona, for a seafood and beer lover, a long lunch in balmy 20 degree conditions was very welcome indeed!

Elsewhere, there were plenty of Arsenal players in action for their countries. Martin Zubimendi played the full 90 minutes for Spain in their 2-0 away win at Czechia. Usually I would wince at a sentence that featured ‘Arsenal player x’ and ‘full 90 minutes’ but I think Zubimendi could use those minutes for physical reasons and for psychological reasons as he tries to plot his way back into a very crowded Arsenal midfield.

Industry observers note that mikel Merino came on for the final 24 minutes of that game and David Raya kept his gloves clean on the bench. Declan Rice played 77 minutes of England’s 2-1 win over Croatia at Wembley in which Harry Kane scored his 417th goal for England, 461 of which have been penalties (citation needed). Eze was an unused sub and he’s another I wouldn’t have minded seeing get some minutes to build rhythm and confidence.

Recent findings suggest that riccardo Calafiori played the full 90 of Italy’s 3-1 win over France. Jurrien Timber and Kai Havertz could be in action tonight as Netherlands play Greece and Germany play away at Serbia. Fingers crossed for both. These are two players I would not mind seeing unused but I doubt that will be the case.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, the major news elsewhere was that Michael Carrick was finally officially sacked by Manchester United. He had still been taking training this week despite everyone knowing that he was for the chop. I hope he filled his coat pockets with as many of the milk and ketchup sachets as he could from the canteen.

According to recent reports, he was clearly out of his depth and had been stalking the United dugout looking like a haunted Noel Gallagher for what feels like months. Steve Holland has also left and Ben White’s recent recall to the England team resurfaced old wounds as he was asked about his reasons for making himself unavailable for a while for his country. White refuses to be drawn on it.

According to recent reports, I am biased, of course, but I know who I think has emerged better from this sorry saga and his surname is a colour not a country. Having taken in Spurs and Chelsea already, it looks like Mauricio Pochettino is about to go three for three on his tour of the Premier League’s most evil institutions. If hell really does exist, this man will regard an eternal stint of fire and brimstone as something of a vacation. Maybe working for the Jim Reaper at United is his penance for accepting work from Chelsea and Spurs.

For further reading, check out my weekly column in which I look at three ways in which Arsenal have evolved this season.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 12:49 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 05:54 EST, 20 November 2026.
  • This time, Matthias Jaissle wants his fingerprints on the bank notes.
  • The need for reinforcement is clear, even on the back of £270million invested in the summer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By CRAIG HOPE, CHIEF FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 12:49 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 05:54 EST, 20 November 2026.

This time, Matthias Jaissle wants his fingerprints on the bank notes. But what the head coach wishes for in January, and what Newcastle United are willing and able to give, is likely to be very different. When that happens, it rarely ends well - on the pitch or off it.

The need for reinforcement is clear, even on the back of £270million invested in the summer. Jaissle knows as much and is not afraid to say so. The rookie German has to protect himself as much as he does his club.

According to recent reports, because, as Newcastle prepare for what threatens to be a long and testing winter, Jaissle is revisiting the brochure presented to him in the summer. And that is the 38-year-old's concern and frustration - the prospectus for the season ahead was not of his making.

He arrived three weeks before the start of the campaign and with four of eight signings already through the door. At a cost of £110m, that quartet have started just three Premier League games between them, and each of those by teenager Sean Steur. Baz Toure and Aladji Bamba are virtual spectators, while reserve keeper Ewen Jaouen is injured.

In a recent development, for Jaissle, you suspect, that money was not spent as he would have advised, had he been in situ. Now, in the new year, he wants greater control, as well as a No 10 and No 9. For any Newcastle follower averse to tension, you best watch this transfer window through your fingertips.

Recent findings suggest that jaissle, sporting director Ross Wilson and chief executive David Hopkinson are the protagonists who will navigate January. At least, that is, if Jaissle makes it into 2027. He deserves that time - not least because of the turbulent and transitional situation he inherited - but the next four fixtures will potentially make or break him and the season.

Head coach Matthias Jaissle is seeking greater control of Newcastle United's transfer strategy.

Aladji Bamba has been a virtual spectator and joined in the summer before Jaissle's arrival.

After the visit of league leaders Arsenal on Saturday, there is a trip to second-placed Brighton, followed by a seismic home double header in the space of five days against Mauricio Pochettino's Manchester United and bitter rivals Sunderland.

It is why, despite rumblings behind the scenes in recent days of potential transfer discord, Jaissle was on message - the collective, club message - when I asked him about the profile of player he might want in January.

Industry observers note that 'It's not the time to talk about the transfer window,' he remarked. 'We have players capable to deliver higher performances on the pitch. We have major quality, not only up front, but throughout the whole squad. We believe we can do better and this is what we now want to influence.'.

In a recent development, however, there was a softening when I sympathised with the head coach over him being judged by a window for which he did not have ownership. Did he, then, want more influence this time?

'Now, it's a different story (compared to the summer), if you're already in and also if you have clarified your clear idea, your clear needs, it's going to be easier,' he mentioned.

In a recent development, 'But the transfer market is still a long time ahead, at least it feels like that right now with our fixtures. Our task, especially from my stance, is to focus on the next match and the upcoming challenges.'.

Jaissle knows that his case will only be strengthened by a steadying of results, even though, conversely, more defeats would heighten the need for signings. They have lost four from six in all competitions.

It has been revealed that the problem is that the hierarchy are on the record as stating the summer business went pretty much exactly as they wished and believed they had a squad for the entire season. There are also Squad Cost Ratio limitations. It is understood there is headroom for one player, but not the two the manager would prefer and not at a fee approaching the £51m they paid for Matias Fernandez-Pardo on deadline day.

Jaissle wants a new No 9 to compete with the likes of Yoane Wisse who has one league goal.

Matias Fernandez-Pardo (left) has failed to impress so far at Newcastle after his £51m arrival.

The 21-year-old forward is another problem. He is still to score from seven appearances and there is a fear he is not yet strong enough for the Premier League. Interestingly, Jaissle revealed on Thursday his dismay that he was booked during the 1-1 draw at Fulham last time out for screaming at Fernandez-Pardo to stand up.

It has been revealed that that is not to say Jaissle does not believe in the talent of those brought in. He does. But for a coach in his first season in a major European league, he needs players who can impact today, not tomorrow. He needs, and wants, more experience. One of his first recommendations in August was to sign 31-year-old midfielder Pierre-Emile Hojbjerg. Nico Gonzalez eventually arrived in that position, but the 24-year-old looks like a player who has spent two seasons in reserve at Manchester City.

Recent findings suggest that so, it is easy to see why Jaissle needs and wants more in January. It is also easy to see why he might not get it. There could be trouble ahead, and that is not just the upcoming matches.

When building a squad it is key to have a vision of the end goal, and AC Milan have exactly that heading into 2027.

Recent findings suggest that la Gazzetta dello Sport begin a report by stating that there are no transition years when it comes to Milan. Frequently they have chosen to overhaul the squad in the summer window, and sometimes even in the winter.

In a recent development, read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

According to recent reports, for example, 2024 brought Paulo Fonseca with Morata, Pavlovic, Fofana, Emerson Royal, Jimenez and Abraham. Then, 2025 brought Gimenez, then Massimiliano Allegri with Modric, Rabiot, Nkunku, Jashari, and De Winter. Last summer brought Ruben Amorim with Ramos, Moreira, Gila, and Cisse.

A not-so-bold prediction: 2027 won’t be slow. Gerry Cardinale even hinted at this, stating: “We’ll continue to be aggressive and opportunistic. It will take a couple more transfer windows to complete everything.” The two transfer windows? Winter and summer, 2027.

The Rossoneri have two key needs right now: a striker and a central defender. They’ll try to secure them as early as the month after next. Nicolo Tresoldi and Endrick are the names that have been talked about for weeks, but the transfer market has surprises.

The difficulties are well known: Club Brugge do not want to sell their jewel in January unless a €60m check materialises, while with Endrick it seems the will of Jose Mourinho must be taken into account. So, alternative names could emerge for the attack.

In a recent development, A central defender is less of a pressing need. Eight months ago, Milan decided to explore the possibility of signing Virgil van Dijk, who turned 35 in July and is regarded as one of the best of his generation.

In a recent development, A year ago, the conditions weren’t there, but now they might be. Van Dijk’s contract expires in June and he’s always been fascinated by Milan and Italy. It’s complex, but it’s worth a try, and Cardinale seems to agree.

According to recent reports, then there is Gabriele Calvani. He’s Italian, 22, plays for Frosinone, and is expected to start San Siro on Sunday. The Diavolo are interested, just as they are keen on Sporting CP’s Gonçalo Inacio, whom Amorim has already coached and attempted to sign in the summer.

Milan will undoubtedly make some changes to their bench over the next 12 months, aiming to mix young players with experienced players. Filippo Terracciano will leave in January, Vladimirov needs to play, Hutchinson is on loan until June, and Jashari will have to reconsider his future.

In a recent development, it’s certain that some Diawara-like players will arrive, i.e. promising prospects chosen through scouting and data. Markus Krösche – if he becomes the latest Head of Football, as is now almost certain – will have extensive powers in this regard.

The idea of ​​making the team more Italian is there, but we know how the market works, making it difficult to proposal. Not only that, but some Italians will soon leave Milan too. Above all, Christian Comotto and Francesco Camarda are heading out on loan.

Industry observers note that the former seems destined for Daniele De Rossi’s Genoa, while it remains to be seen where and under what terms the altter will leave. A loan with an option to buy, leaving Milan free to control the future, probably. To a small Serie A team? Possibly, but a move abroad is possible too.

Belgium and the Netherlands are countries where strikers historically have more opportunities in teams that are younger, while Germany could be another destination. If he takes a flight north, don’t be surprised.

Breaking: An Arseblog upgrade

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1163 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it’s around 10.30am on Friday, November 6th 2026.
  • It has been revealed that my phone rings.
  • “Can you come into us on Monday afternoon at 2.30?”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it’s around 10.30am on Friday, November 6th 2026. I’m in my hotel room in London, doing a few Arseblog bits on my laptop, and getting ready for the launch of the The 22 in the Big Red that night.

It has been revealed that my phone rings. It’s a Dublin number but one not in my contacts. Typically I wouldn’t answer, but I think I know who it probably is. I’m right. It’s the Oncology department of the hospital I was admitted to a couple of weeks ago. They have news.

“We have the results of your biopsy.”.

“Can you come into us on Monday afternoon at 2.30?”.

“Great, we’ll see you then. Oh, and you should bring somebody with you. It’s a lot of information to take in.”.

As of this moment, I’m still not 100% on all the details. I had another scan yesterday, and I have a procedure scheduled for Tuesday which will give us more information. However, they’ve already laid out a plan for three months of chemo, which is kind of why I’m writing this.

Recent findings suggest that my very, very strong instinct with any medical stuff is to keep it private. And I suppose if I was a guy who had a regular 9 to 5 and went to the office every day, I could do that. However, the privilege of my work is that it is very public facing. I do the stuff, you read the stuff and listen to the stuff, and you are part of my life in a very big way; in the same way – even if it it’s just for a few minutes each morning, or a couple of hours in your headphones – that I’m part of yours.

Sources indicate that which isn’t say I feel like I owe anyone an explanation, but this is my reality now, and for what’s likely to be an arduous road ahead for a while. Unfortunately, that makes it part of your reality too. I will say, I’m not going to document my ‘journey’. Fair play to anyone who does. Whatever you need to do to get through the challenges an illness presents, it’s just not really who I am. I don’t even do video on podcasts about football, so I’m not gonna start now for something like this!

But I do need the distraction of work, of Arsenal, of football and all its ludicrousness and drama, and this incredible community that has grown over the near 25 years of Arseblog’s existence. I’ve missed it this week, despite the fact it’s been such a difficult time in this household. We’ve gone through all the normal human reactions and emotions, and the whole thing was compounded by the fact I came back from London with the single worst stomach bug I’ve ever had in my life. To be honest, that felt a bit mean from the universe. Here, have a bit of this, and just to make you feel worse, you will require about twenty visits to the bathroom every day. It’s a bit like one of those days where every set of traffic lights you hit turns red as you approach, but the traffic lights also make your arse hurt. Fuck off!

So, I’m going to be around, and I’m gonna do my best to do what I normally do. I need as much normal as I can get, because right now too much isn’t. But there will be days when I’m not, or I can’t be, and I’m happy to let the lads pick up the slack as much as possible. To preempt many messages and thoughts, I know what the priority is, and I’m not going to push myself at the expense of my health or getting better. I have a vested interest in, you know, making a full recovery. I’m not going to risk doing anything that might conflict with that.

But I also feel like the best way to navigate this is to not let it take over my life, or to define who I am. I’m still just an Irish bloke with a website about Arsenal first and foremost, and the last week or so has made me feel strangely protective of that. A dose of perspective is a really interesting thing, I know what the most vital thing is right now, but that can only succeed if I remain myself. I hope that makes sense.

Recent findings suggest that some lads kicking a ball around a football pitch is, in the grand scheme of things, not that crucial. But hasn’t that always been the case? Football is so intrinsic to all of us, and we give so much of our time and energy to it, because we (well most of us) understand the absurdity of giving so much of ourselves to something that is completely out of our control. We can pretend otherwise, but that’s all part of the fun too. Lucky socks and lucky shirts and matchday routines. Our brain’s way of trying to make it feel like we have some influence, because we need that sliver of pretence, but in the end it’s about whether some millionaire at the back post can apply the finish.

It has been revealed that I suppose at least this shit waited until there was an Interlull. Thanks for that.

I’m lucky because I have an amazing wife and daughter, and family and friends, who will be with me every step of the way. Their support thus far has been incredible, and I know I can count on it 100%. I’m going to listen to the doctors and the medical team and do whatever it is they ask of me. They seem to know what they’re on about, which is reassuring. Almost like they’re experts or something. We should listen to them.

I know as well that wider support from the Arseblog community will be forthcoming, and I just wanted to say in advance that I appreciate it hugely. I suspect that replying to every message is going to be beyond me, and in normal circumstances that would bother me greatly. I always try to respond to every email I get, even if it takes me a while, but in this instance I hope you’ll understand if I don’t or can’t.

In a recent development, so that’s where we are. I still don’t know where we’ll end up or how we’ll get there, but despite the fact I’m scared and worried, I’m also positive and determined. I could really do without this, to be quite honest, but it is what it is, and the only way through is forward. I’ll keep you in the loop as much as I feel I can, and in the meantime if Arsenal could make my day to day life as stress free as possible, I’d really appreciate that.

Someone have a word with Mikel and the lads.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Anthony Nolan | 20 Nov 2026 23:59, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 04:57.

Werder Bremen will be battling to keep their unlikely European dream alive on Sunday, when they welcome Hamburger SV to the Weserstadion for a Bundesliga Nordderby.

Die Werderaner are hoping to bounce back from defeat last time out, while HSV are keen to pick up where they left off prior to the international break.

Daniel Thioune guided Werder to safety last term after taking the helm in early February, though his sights are set much higher this time around with his team sat in a strong position upon the league's return.

Nine matches into the campaign, Die Werderaner are sixth in the Bundesliga table, where their tally of 15 points has them two clear of seventh-placed Elversberg and just three shy of RB Leipzig in fourth.

Securing European football of any variety would be a major accomplishment for Thioune, who is right now in his first top-flight role as manager, not to mention that the club last appeared on the continental stage back in the 2010-11 Champions League group stage.

However, Werder signed off for the international break with a 1-0 defeat at Stuttgart on November 7, their second loss in three matches after a 3-2 beating by Borussia Dortmund in the DFB-Pokal in late October.

In fairness to the Green-Whites, they fought back from 2-0 down against BVB thanks to a brace from Niclas Fullkrug, only to lose out to a stoppage-time free kick by Marcel Sabitzer.

Additionally, a 2-0 victory over Hoffenheim between those defeats saw the hosts maintain their unbeaten streak on home turf this season, where they will hope to record a fourth win in five outings on Sunday.

Meanwhile, Merlin Polzin's Hamburger endured a dire start to the season, conceding 12 goals without reply in their first three Bundesliga games before firing back with a run of three consecutive triumphs.

It would be fair to say that HSV's term has been defined by streaks so far, alternating between trios of defeats and wins across all competitions, and the club will be hoping to stabilise after the international break.

Polzin's side were held to a 1-1 draw by Croatia's Hajduk Split in a friendly on November 15, following up a 3-1 success against Borussia Monchengladbach that helped to distance the team from the relegation zone in the German top flight.

That victory has left Hamburger 11th in the Bundesliga table with 12 points to their name - a total that puts them level with Eintracht Frankfurt, Hoffenheim and Stuttgart up to eighth - as well as five points clear of 16th-placed Union Berlin.

Earning another win on Sunday would be keeping with HSV's pattern this term, but after seeing the visitors lose four of their five away league matches in 2026-27, fans would be forgiven for harbouring doubts.

Werder Bremen form (all competitions):.

Hamburger SV form (all competitions):.

Werder will be without strikers Keke Topp (ACL) and Salim Musah (thigh) once again as they recover from long-term injuries, though the doubts about Marco Grull's fitness after he missed training with a calf problem will be a major concern for the team.

If Grull is sidelined on Sunday, then expect to see Niclas Fullkrug supported up top by Eren Dinkci, Chuki and Justin Njinmah.

Jens Stage and Skelly Alvero are also unavailable due to respective thigh and calf injuries, while question marks remain about the readiness of fellow midfielder Senne Lynen, who has been ill over the past week, though Youri Regeer and Ludovit Reis should be on hand to form Thioune's double pivot.

Elsewhere, the versatile Mitchell Weiser is a doubt with a thigh problem and left-back Moussa N'Diaye is recovering from a groin injury, so Arthur and Olivier Deman look set to start at full-back.

As for Hamburger, they are missing centre-back Jordan Torunarigha, who has been dealing with a hip issue, but Mario Vuskovic is likely to return after getting over a minor back injury.

The visitors are lighter in midfield than ideal, with all three of Albert Sambi Lokonga (calf), Bilal Nadir (thigh) and Nicolai Remberg (ACL) sidelined, so Martin Adeline could join Miro Muheim in the centre of the park, while Albert Gronbaek operates in the number 10 role.

Centre-forward Yussuf Poulsen is also out with a calf injury, but Terem Moffi and Patson Daka will be ready to lead the line in a strike partnership on Sunday.

Werder Bremen possible starting lineup:.

Hein; Arthur, Friedl, Pieper, Deman; Regeer, Reis; Dinkci, Chuki, Njinmah; Fullkrug.

Hamburger SV possible starting lineup:.

Heuer; Capaldo, Omari, Bornauw; El Ouahdi, Adeline, Muheim, Moller Wolfe; Gronbaek; Moffi, Daka.

Werder have been exceptional on home turf this season, and they will be expecting to collect all three points once again, but the match is likely to be closer than otherwise if Grull remains sidelined.

By contrast, Hamburger have struggled on the road throughout 2026-27, and with four defeats in five away Bundesliga games so far, expect to see the visitors' overall pattern of results broken.

💡 Key Takeaways
