Conservation of the tumour microenvironment across organs and species

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 90 min read (17938 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~90 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, current understanding of the host tissue response to solid tumours is largely based on investigations of tumour types in isolation1.
  • Solid-organ cancers represent a complex spectrum of pathology, with the intricately associated TME having a pivotal role in disease progression and therapeutic response4,5.
  • Recent findings suggest that previous studies have identified distinct cell subpopulations within the TME based on their gene expression profiles, spatial distributions and functional characteristics17,18,19,20,21.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, current understanding of the host tissue response to solid tumours is largely based on investigations of tumour types in isolation1. Given the breadth and diversity of human tumour pathology and contributions of tumour microenvironment (TME) cells to disease progression, pan-cancer analysis is needed to bridge major themes of stromal and immune cell evolution. To date, however, efforts to compare the TME response across cancers have been limited in scope2,3. Here we conduct a comprehensive pan-cancer analysis by algorithmically screening thousands of publicly available single-cell transcriptomic datasets for stromal and immune signatures across species and tissue types. We demonstrate conserved hallmarks of host cell transcriptional programming in response to malignancy across 42 cancer types in more than 2,000 human and mouse tumour samples. These findings are codified as an interactive web atlas (tmeatlas.stanford.edu) and software package (scTME) that will serve as practical resources for the systematic interrogation of the TME in tumours.

Solid-organ cancers represent a complex spectrum of pathology, with the intricately associated TME having a pivotal role in disease progression and therapeutic response4,5. Within the TME, both stromal and immune cells have emerged as key modulators of tumour growth, invasion and metastasis1,6,7,8,9,10. However, different studies (often in single-organ contexts) have shown conflicting roles for these cells in promoting versus suppressing tumour growth11,12,13,14. The heterogeneity of the TME, both within individual tumours and across tumour types, poses a substantial challenge to understanding the functional diversity of tumour-associated stromal and immune cells3,15,16.

Recent findings suggest that previous studies have identified distinct cell subpopulations within the TME based on their gene expression profiles, spatial distributions and functional characteristics17,18,19,20,21. However, these findings stem largely from isolated single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies22,23,24, and subsequent pan-cancer efforts have remained limited in size and scope3,25,26,27,28. To our knowledge, the largest cancer-associated fibroblast atlas to date integrates data from 1,116 samples across 10 tumour types29; the largest tumour endothelial cell atlas includes 575 samples across 19 tumour types30; and no specific tumour mural or nerve atlases have been generated. Pan-cancer immune cell atlases have been larger28, especially those focused on individual immune cell lineages31,32,33; however, these typically have not examined immune cell interactions within the broader TME.

Here we integrated single-cell transcriptomic data from 3,381 human and mouse samples across 42 cancer types and 258 datasets to create a definitive TME transcriptional atlas. By mapping this massive cellular landscape, we resolved the stromal and immune ecosystem of solid tumours. Furthermore, by linking enriched subpopulations to poor clinical outcomes, we identified opportunities for future TME-targeted cancer therapies. Key computational predictions are subsequently validated through in vitro and in vivo experiments. Finally, we have consolidated this work into an interactive web atlas (tmeatlas.stanford.edu) and R software package (scTME) that will serve as practical resources for groups investigating the TME.

According to recent reports, to systematically analyse single-cell transcriptomic data, we evaluated every scRNA-seq cancer study published in the public domain between January 2014 and July 2025. Separate queries were evaluated independently for human and mouse datasets within the foundational public repositories for single-cell transcriptomics: the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and ArrayExpress. We screened a total of 3,975 published datasets (Fig. 1a). Studies specific to either blood or central nervous system cancers were excluded from our analysis, as were those failing to meet specific architectural requirements (Methods; see Fig. 1a,b). Our comprehensive screen identified 190 human and 68 mouse datasets (Supplementary Table 1), collectively comprising more than 15.4 million cells. Collectively, these datasets formed the final analytical cohort, comprising 3,381 individual scRNA-seq samples across 42 unique cancer types (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Tables 2 and 3).

In a recent development, a, Systematic workflow detailing the scRNA-seq dataset curation process. The initial screen examined 3,975 datasets, of which 190 human and 68 mouse scRNA-seq remained after filtering. The combined 258 datasets comprised 3,381 samples and more than 15 million cells. Schematic created in BioRender; Wang, H. https://biorender.com/w8x4pii (2026). CNS, central nervous system. b, Illustration of all cancer types from human (top) and mouse (bottom) included in this study. HNSCC, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma; MPNST, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour; NSCLC, non-small-cell lung cancer; SCLC, small-cell lung cancer. Illustration created in BioRender; Wang, H. https://biorender.com/p0byno1 (2026).

To process the more than 12.8 million human cells from 2,855 samples and 190 datasets (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b and Supplementary Fig. 1), nearly an order of magnitude greater than many recent seminal studies3,25,26,27,28,31,32,33,34, we used sketch-based sampling and memory read optimization (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d). We applied three independent approaches for data integration to reduce batch effects: Harmony, scVI and FastMNN (Extended Data Figs. 1e and 2a). We then projected each integrated result onto the full dataset (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). Supervised annotation using four methods—canonical marker genes, estimated copy number variation (inferCNV), SingleR and scATOMIC (Extended Data Fig. 3 and Supplementary Fig. 2)—delineated the presence of seven main cell types across nearly all human cancers (Fig. 2a–c, Extended Data Fig. 1e,f and Supplementary Table 4). These encompass principal stromal (fibroblast, endothelial, mural and nerve) and immune (myeloid and lymphoid) lineages, alongside epithelial cells, which were excluded from subsequent characterization to focus on the two core TME compartments. Comparing the three integration approaches (Supplementary Table 5), Harmony demonstrated the most robust integration and was selected for all subsequent evaluations. The three integration approaches also frequently yielded discordant cell-type assignments for individual cells (Extended Data Fig. 2d–f), highlighting the stochasticity and misclassification risks inherent to relying on any single method35,36. To mitigate this, we provisionally pooled all cells assigned to a specific TME lineage by any of the three algorithms (Extended Data Fig. 1g). Misassigned cells within these overlapping pools were subsequently removed through recursive downstream filtering (Extended Data Fig. 1h and Supplementary Fig. 3a–e), generating final, high-fidelity atlases for the six principal TME cell types (Fig. 2d–i and Extended Data Fig. 1i,j).

Industry observers note that a, UMAP embeddings of 12,855,771 cells from 190 human studies integrated using Harmony, with consensus seven cell-type annotations (outlined and labelled within the panel) derived through multiple annotation approaches (Extended Data Figs. 1 and 2 and Supplementary Figs. 1–3). Individual cells are labelled according to downstream final cell annotations in panels d–i. cDC, conventional dendritic cell; DC, dendritic cell; End, endothelial; Fib, fibroblast; Lym, lymphoid; Mac, macrophage; mem, memory; Mono, monocyte; mregDC, mature dendritic cell enriched in immunoregulatory molecules; Mur, mural; myel, myelinating; Myl, myeloid; Neut, neutrophil; NK, natural killer; SMC, smooth muscle cell; TFH, follicular helper T; Treg, regulatory T. b, Total number of human samples included for each type of cancer. c, Distribution of cell types for each cancer, after selecting for only unsorted samples. Abbreviations of cancer names are listed in Supplementary Table 2. d, UMAP embedding of CAFs, manually clustered into four parent populations (outlined and labelled within the UMAP) from a total of seven transcriptionally distinct subpopulations, the latter of which are coloured separately (top left). A dot plot displaying relative gene expression for characteristic markers of the seven transcriptionally distinct CAF subpopulations shown in the left panel (top right). Distributions of CAF subpopulations among tumour samples for different cancer types are also shown (bottom; n = 328,877 cells). e–i, UMAPs (top left), dot plots (top right) and distributions among tumour samples for different cancer types (bottom) for endothelial (e; n = 234,948 cells), mural (f; n = 162,178 cells), nerve (g; n = 7,655 cells), lymphoid (h; n = 1,580,785 cells) and myeloid (i; n = 805,111 cells) cells. Between 3 and 12 subpopulations are identified for each cell type, and one population-defining gene per subpopulation is displayed in the dot plot for each cell type (full list in Supplementary Tables 6 and 7).

We next characterized cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), the predominant stromal population in the TME37. Following our recursive isolation strategy (Extended Data Fig. 1h), we delineated four transcriptionally distinct CAF meta-clusters (Fig. 2d) expressing canonical markers (PDGFRA, LUM and DCN) and lacking non-fibroblast markers (Extended Data Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 4). Specifically, we identified (1) antigen-presenting CAFs (apCAFs; class II HLA+), (2) immunomodulatory/inflammatory CAFs (iCAFs; cytokine+), (3) myofibroblastic/mechanoresponsive CAFs (mCAFs; extracellular matrix (ECM)+, mechanotransduction+), and (4) steady-state CAFs (ssCAFs; progenitor-like markers+; Fig. 2d), broadly consistent with observations from our previous work38 and that of others25,39,40,41. High-resolution sub-clustering (Fig. 2d, Supplementary Table 6 and 7 and Supplementary Fig. 4) further stratified these into seven subpopulations: two iCAF (CXCL8+ or ISG15+), two mCAF (LRRC15+ or COL4A1+), two ssCAF (PI16+ or CXCL14+) and one apCAF. All seven subpopulations were conserved across nearly all evaluated tumour types and tissues (Fig. 2d, bottom). Of note, apCAFs were nearly universally present, whereas previous studies had found them only in rare tumour subsets6. Furthermore, the human apCAFs that we identified did not express mesothelial markers such as MSLN, which are characteristic of mouse apCAFs42 (Extended Data Fig. 4a).

According to recent reports, comparing relative abundances between tumour and non-malignant tissues (Fig. 3a), both mCAF populations were significantly enriched in tumours (3.5-fold for LRRC15+; 2.7-fold for COL4A1+; Supplementary Table 8), reflecting cancer-induced desmoplasia37,43. Similarly, iCAFs and apCAFs were enriched in tumour samples (6.3-fold for ISG15+ iCAFs, 1.3-fold for CXCL8+ iCAFs and 2.0-fold for apCAFs), consistent with their roles in inducing immune evasion42 or secreting inflammatory cytokines41. Analysing abundance across tumour stage and patient treatment response, we found ISG15+ iCAFs, LRRC15+ mCAFs and COL4A1+ mCAFs significantly enriched in late-stage (III–IV) versus early-stage (I–II) tumours (1.9-fold, 1.3-fold and 1.2-fold, respectively; Fig. 3b). Treatment responsiveness did not significantly correlate with any CAF subpopulation (Fig. 3c). Overall, ISG15+ iCAFs were the most consistently enriched fibroblast subset defining both the malignant state and advanced disease (Fig. 3a–c, blue box).

In a recent development, a–c, Forest plots of cell subpopulation proportions, relative to their parent population, between tumour and non-malignant samples (a), advanced-stage (3–4) versus early-stage (1–2) cancer (b), and treatment non-responders versus responders (c). The blue box in panel a highlights ISG15+ iCAFs. Non-malignant samples comprise tissue resected adjacent to a tumour, pooled with tissue from individuals or animals without tumours. The points show fold enrichment, the ratio of weighted mean per-sample proportions; the unit of replication is the individual scRNA-seq sample, weighted by the square root of its cell number. The error bars show the propagated standard error of that ratio (see Methods). Significance was determined by two-sided weighted Welch t-tests, with Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment within each parent lineage; the colour denotes adjusted P < 0.05. All samples are biologically independent; n = 859–1,777 (a), 311–658 (b) and 48–108 (c) samples per parent lineage. Exact n, group means, standard errors, fold enrichments with 95% confidence intervals, test statistics and exact P values are provided in Supplementary Table 8. d, Immunofluorescence for apCAFs (PDGFRα+HLA-DR+ co-staining) in tumour and matched tumour-adjacent tissue from PDAC, CRC and PTC. The white boxes mark co-staining. n = 7 PDAC, 3 CRC and 3 PTC biologically independent specimens; each was stained and imaged once, with comparable patterns within each tumour type. Scale bars, 100 µm. e, Pseudotemporal manifold from a published PDAC dataset62, with yellow indicating ECM regions of high pseudotime and blue showing low pseudotime (left). UMAP is coloured by overall survival; higher pseudotime accompanies shorter survival (right). f, PDAC tissue microarray with haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining (left) and ECM pseudotime (right); the blue and yellow boxes mark the low-pseudotime and high-pseudotime regions shown in panels g,h. Scale bar, 200 µm. g,h, Histology and CODEX of those regions with low matrix pseudotime and good patient survival (g) and high matrix pseudotime and poor patient survival (h). H&E (top left); remaining panels, CODEX for the indicated markers. The white boxes mark putative apCAFs: HLA-DR+ spindle-like cells in areas of high COL1A1/αSMA expression without tumour or other immune markers. CODEX was performed on n = 3 biologically independent PDAC specimens, each analysed once in a single multiplexed run. Scale bars, 50 µm.

Industry observers note that focusing on the iCAF compartment, our atlas revealed two distinct and conserved transcriptional states: ISG15+ iCAFs exhibiting canonical interferon-γ (IFNγ) stimulation (for example, CXCL10)44, and CXCL8+ iCAFs expressing pro-inflammatory cytokines (for example, CXCL1)41. Crucially, these iCAF subpopulations provide additional granularity compared with previously reported CXCL12+ iCAFs39. Recent consensus frameworks have identified CXCL12 to be among the steady-state fibroblast hallmark genes rather than specific to a malignancy-induced inflammatory CAF state25. In line with this, our CXCL14+ ssCAFs co-expressed high levels of CXCL12 while maintaining a homeostatic signature. Abundance analyses revealed divergent ssCAF dynamics: conventional PI16+ ssCAFs (which also strongly express CXCL12) were heavily enriched in non-malignant tissue (2.8-fold), potentially representing a progenitor pool, whereas the CXCL14+ pool remained proportionally stable across benign and malignant tissues (1.0-fold), typifying embedded parenchymal fibroblasts. We therefore propose that traditional ‘CXCL12+ iCAFs’ are more accurately classified as tissue-resident CXCL14+ ssCAFs.

To elucidate the regulatory networks driving these distinct states, we examined transcription factor activity using SCENIC. The apCAF population exhibited elevated inferred activity of RUNX3 and IKZF1, regulators of MHC class II expression45, suggesting a mechanism for direct T cell interaction and immunotherapy resistance (Extended Data Fig. 5a). The ISG15+ iCAFs demonstrated predicted activation of ETV7 and IRF2, implicating suppressive cytokine signalling in tumour progression46 (Extended Data Fig. 5b). Both mCAF populations were enriched for CREB3L1 and NKX3-2, linked to ECM overexpression and stiffness (Extended Data Fig. 5c). Conversely, ssCAF populations exhibited higher predicted activity of CEBPA and FOXO3, which regulate lineage and redox homeostasis, respectively, consistent with the homeostatic properties ascribed to this population26 (Extended Data Fig. 5d). Overall, these regulatory profiles broadly align with the putative functional roles attributed to each CAF subpopulation.

Recent findings suggest that to evaluate whether specific populations could be distinguished by differences in metabolic programs, we applied scMetabolism to analyse our scRNA-seq dataset. Of note, we observed that LRRC15+ mCAFs were enriched for genes associated with elevated oxidative phosphorylation, in contrast to the traditional glycolytic programs of ISG15+ iCAFs (Extended Data Fig. 5e,f and Supplementary Fig. 5a–c). These profiles align with the distinct energy demands of each cell type: iCAFs expressed genes linked with rapid glycolytic ATP generation that would permit overproduction of pro-inflammatory cytokines, whereas mCAFs were predicted to utilize the more efficient oxidative phosphorylation, enabling them to sustain intense ECM production and remodelling driving the desmoplastic response to neoplasia47. ssCAFs exhibited globally lower expression of metabolic pathway genes, reinforcing their relatively quiescent state.

To determine whether these distinct functional and metabolic states ultimately impact patient survival, we paired bulk RNA-seq and clinical outcome data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) using CIBERSORTx deconvolution (Supplementary Table 9 and Supplementary Fig. 6a,b). Patients whose tumours were estimated to have higher abundances of apCAFs, iCAFs or mCAFs exhibited worse overall survival across most cancer types, consistent with previous observations48. By contrast, we observed a positive (but not statistically significant; 1.3-fold, P = 0.27) relationship between CXCL14+ ssCAF proportion and patient survival. Together, these results suggest that fibroblast differentiation and lineage progression may be associated with worse outcomes in solid-organ tumours, reflecting a pro-tumorigenic role for apCAFs, iCAFs and mCAFs.

It has been revealed that beyond fibroblasts, we examined tumour endothelial, mural and nerve cells, which drive angiogenesis, cytokine signalling and metastatic spread1,7,8,49. In silico isolation of endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 1a–j) identified five pan-cancer subpopulations (Fig. 2e): GJA5+ arterial, CA4+ capillary, PROX1+ lymphatic, ESM1+ tip and ACKR1+ venous. All expressed canonical markers (PECAM1, VWF and CDH5) and lacked non-endothelial signatures (Extended Data Fig. 4b, Supplementary Table 6 and Supplementary Fig. 7). Of note, angiogenic ESM1+ tip cells50 were the sole endothelial subpopulation significantly enriched in tumours versus non-malignant tissue (1.7-fold; Fig. 3a and Supplementary Table 8), reflecting dysfunctional tumour neovascularization51. These tip cells, co-expressing FLT1 (VEGFR1) and KDR (VEGFR2), were significantly elevated in treatment non-responsive tumours (1.9-fold; Fig. 3c). Furthermore, they correlated with elevated metabolic activity (Extended Data Fig. 5g and Supplementary Fig. 5d) and worse overall survival across most TCGA cohorts (Supplementary Fig. 6b). These data reinforce the pro-tumorigenic role of tip cells7,52,53, which may continuously support growth by rapidly initiating marginal angiogenesis, highlighting them as candidate targets for multi-drug therapy.

Sources indicate that subclustering of pan-cancer mural cells delineated six distinct subpopulations (Fig. 2f): CCL2+, CD248+ and ISG15+ pericytes; RERGL+ and WFDC1+ vascular smooth muscle cells; and DES+ visceral smooth muscle cells. All expressed canonical markers (RGS5, PDGFRB and CSPG4) and lacked non-mural signatures (Supplementary Table 6 and Supplementary Fig. 8). ISG15+ and CD248+ pericytes, alongside WFDC1+ vascular smooth muscle cells, were significantly enriched in tumours versus non-malignant tissue (4.5-fold, 1.8-fold and 1.2-fold, respectively; Fig. 3a and Supplementary Table 8), with ISG15+ pericytes also exhibiting elevated overall metabolic activity (Extended Data Fig. 5h). Clinically, CD248+ pericytes correlated with poor treatment response (1.8-fold; Fig. 3c). Mechanistically, both tumour-enriched pericyte populations expressed ECM genes (COL1A1, COL3A1 and COL4A1), supporting a role in tumour desmoplasia (Supplementary Fig. 5e,f). Of note, PIEZO2, which encodes a mechanotransduction channel, was detected in a small subset of CD248+ pericytes and was not detected in other mural populations (Supplementary Fig. 8). Detection was sparse and expression levels were low, indicating selective rather than robust population-specific expression. Given the established role of PIEZO2 in cellular mechanosensation54, we hypothesize that this fraction of pro-fibrotic pericytes may be activated by the stiffened TME to further upregulate ECM production, a possibility that merits further investigation.

Recent findings suggest that finally, we analysed tumour-associated nerve cells, filtering out neural crest cancers to avoid transcriptional overlap with nerve-based tumours49. Our analysis revealed three distinct subpopulations and their canonical markers: MLANA+ melanocytes, MPZ+ myelinating Schwann cells and NGFR+ non-myelinating Schwann cells (Fig. 2g, Supplementary Table 6 and Supplementary Fig. 9). Subpopulation proportions varied markedly across tumour types (Fig. 2g, bottom). Because this heterogeneity probably reflects both tissue-specific neural architecture and the general rarity of nerve cells in standard biopsies, these populations were omitted from subsequent downstream analyses.

Recent findings suggest that comprising over 2.4 million cells, immune cells constituted the largest TME compartment in our atlas. In silico isolation broadly segregated these into lymphoid and myeloid lineages. Focusing first on lymphoid cells—primary mediators of antitumour immunity55—we identified 11 subpopulations: CD4+ (3) and CD8+ (3) T cells, natural killer cells (1), B cells (3) and plasma cells (1; Fig. 2h, Supplementary Table 6 and Supplementary Fig. 10). Nearly all T cell populations were significantly enriched in tumours (Fig. 3a). This was driven primarily by CD8+ISG15+ IFN-primed T cells (2.4-fold) and CD8+GZMB+ tumour-reactive exhausted T (TEX) cells (1.5-fold). Of note, this GZMB+ population was also significantly enriched in early-stage disease (Fig. 3b), reflecting an initial wave of localized antitumour immunity undergoing rapid, chronic antigen-driven dysfunction56. In addition, FOXP3+ regulatory T cells (1.8-fold) and CXCL13+ follicular helper T cells (1.6-fold) were both enriched in tumours. By contrast, B cell and plasma populations were comparatively depleted within the tumour but enriched in non-malignant tissue, probably reflecting peritumoural accumulation and immune exclusion from the tumour core57.

It has been revealed that examining tumour myeloid cells, we identified dendritic cells (three populations), monocytes (two populations), macrophages (four populations), mast cells, neutrophils and osteoclasts (Fig. 2i, Supplementary Table 6 and Supplementary Fig. 11). Most spanned all tumour types, except the tissue-specific osteoclasts (Fig. 2i, bottom). Three macrophage subtypes and LAMP3+ mature immunoregulatory dendritic cells were significantly tumour enriched (Fig. 3a), with SPP1+ and MARCO+ subpopulations further enriched in late-stage disease (Fig. 3b). SPP1+ macrophages (GPNMB+ and APOC1+) are known drivers of desmoplasia and poor clinical outcomes32, whereas late-stage MARCO+ enrichment suggests a specialized role in immunosuppression and hindered phagocytosis. Conversely, C1QC+ macrophages maintain a homeostatic, complement-rich signature (C1QA–C and FOLR2) linked to T cell infiltration and a non-exhausted TME58. LAMP3+ mature immunoregulatory dendritic cells (IDO1+ and CCR7+) represent a critical regulatory checkpoint, limiting cytotoxic T cell activity to facilitate late-stage immune evasion59. Finally, shared ISG15+ ‘IFN-primed’ clusters across both macrophages and T cells suggest a common axis of chronic inflammation driving terminal exhaustion via sustained type I IFN signalling31,32.

It has been revealed that to evaluate alignment with broader transcriptional consensus models, we performed quantitative cell-level comparisons against four pan-cancer reference atlases using pairwise expression mapping via our scTME software package60 (Extended Data Fig. 6a–d). Most of our subpopulations exhibited strong, reciprocal alignment with comparable cell types across datasets (for example, PI16+ ssCAFs, LRRC15+ mCAFs, ESM1+ tip cells, C1QC+/SPP1+ macrophages and FOXP3+ regulatory T cells). These comparisons also differentiated several of our newly characterized and finely partitioned subpopulations. The IFN-primed (ISG15+) axis mapped robustly to analogous IFN-activated states across lineages (Extended Data Fig. 6b). In addition, our newly identified ISG15+ pericytes mapped to parent pericytes (Extended Data Fig. 6a) but diverged from CD248+ pericytes in broader TME atlases by lacking myofibroblast overlap, reinforcing their distinct state (Extended Data Fig. 6c,d). Furthermore, CXCL14+ fibroblasts mapped predominantly to non-inflammatory populations—unlike the CXCL8+ and ISG15+ iCAF subpopulations—supporting their separation from canonical iCAFs. Overall, although our TME atlas is broadly congruent with established datasets, our fibroblast and mural subpopulations reflect a uniquely refined, data-driven partitioning with functional relevance.

It has been revealed that our meta-analysis identified apCAFs across nearly all evaluated tumour types (Fig. 2d, bottom), far exceeding the limited number of cancers in which they have been validated in vivo6. Therefore, we performed immunohistochemistry to confirm their presence in previously uncharacterized tumour types. Co-staining for the membranous fibroblast marker PDGFRα and the antigen-presenting marker HLA-DR confirmed apCAF presence in human pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) controls61, as well as in previously non-validated colorectal cancer (CRC) and papillary thyroid cancer (PTC) tissues, as predicted by our atlas (Fig. 3d). To exclude possible immune cell misclassification, we analysed multiplexed spatial proteomic (CODEX) data from human PDAC62. Spindle-like HLA-DR+ cells localized to highly fibrotic (COL1A1+/αSMA+) regions, lacked immune or epithelial markers (Fig. 3g,h), and occupied distinct ECM architectures associated with poor patient outcomes (Fig. 3e,f and Supplementary Fig. 12a–f). We further orthogonally validated apCAF presence using public Xenium spatial transcriptomic datasets63,64 (Supplementary Fig. 13a–c). scRNA-seq revealed only a modest correlation between apCAF and T cell abundances in tumour samples (Supplementary Fig. 14a), suggesting that apCAF expansion occurs regional to but independent of direct T cell support. By contrast, ISG15+ iCAFs strongly correlated with CD8+ISG15+ IFN-primed T cells (Supplementary Fig. 14b), supporting our hypothesis that this CAF population interacts with T cells to drive exhaustion and promote immune evasion.

Recent findings suggest that to infer interaction networks, we paired CellChat receptor–ligand predictions with orthogonal NicheNet modelling of downstream transcriptional targets. Because multiple lineages harboured ISG15+ clusters, we first evaluated the IFNγ network. CellChat predicted robust signalling from CD8+GZMB+ tumour-reactive TEX cells to ISG15+ iCAFs (Fig. 4a), which was corroborated by NicheNet (Fig. 4b). These aligned predictions support the hypothesis that ISG15+ iCAFs act as direct responders to chronic, T cell-derived IFNγ within the TME. Applying this approach to explore drivers of dysfunctional neovascularization, CellChat predicted that ESM1+ endothelial tip cells receive disproportionately high VEGF signalling from tumour-associated macrophages and monocytes (Extended Data Fig. 7a). NicheNet further corroborated this relationship (Extended Data Fig. 7b), successfully recapitulating this established myeloid-driven angiogenic axis using data solely from our atlas65. Conversely, NicheNet did not directly substantiate several other CellChat-predicted receptor–ligand pairings as transcriptional drivers, suggesting that these specific interactions may operate via indirect or non-transcriptional mechanisms (Extended Data Fig. 7c,d and Supplementary Fig. 15a–d).
